soil-phys-001.title: How grains and gaps build a living soil
soil-phys-001.text: A farmer cannot change the mineral grains in a field, but can wreck or rebuild the way they fit together. That arrangement is soil structure: how a soil's solid particles sit, and the pore spaces left between them. Texture is innate, fixed by the mineral particles themselves, the separates described in {{ref:soil-phys-047}}. Structure is not. It depends on how particles clump, bind and gather into aggregates, small crumbs of particles stuck together. Those clumps in turn set the pattern of pores. Through that pattern, structure shapes how water and air move, how heat travels, and how roots and seedlings push through. It also governs biological activity and how well the soil resists erosion. Structure never sits still. Tillage, wheel traffic, roots, microbes and soil animals reshape it, and so do rain, wind, wetting and drying, and freezing and thawing. Most cultivation does harm. Mechanical mixing compacts and shears aggregates, fills pores and exposes organic matter to faster decay. Continued cultivation and traffic can press compacted, impermeable layers called hardpans into the soil profile. Irrigation brings its own damage, as aggregates break apart and clay disperses on rapid wetting. Sodic soils suffer most, because sodium makes wet particles push one another apart. Yet the choice and timing of farming practices can improve structure as well as destroy it. Read with care, structure is also a record. It holds clues to a soil's texture, organic matter, biology, history and human use, and to the chemistry under which it formed.

soil-phys-003.title: Peds: the natural building blocks of soil
soil-phys-003.text: A lump of earth gets a different name depending on who made it. When soil-forming processes build it, it is a ped: a natural aggregate of soil particles, set apart from its neighbors by pores or voids. When cultivation makes it, it is merely a clod. The word, a contraction of pedolith, is used mostly for visible units larger than 1 mm seen in the field. Peds form as sand, silt and clay clump into aggregates, and aggregates clump into larger units. Coatings of iron oxides, carbonates, clay, silica and humus glue them into fairly stable secondary structures. Some soils are structureless, while others have simple units or compound units built of smaller ones. The gaps between peds are one way large pores, or macropores, form, alongside roots, cracks and soil animals. Peds are best described when soil is dry or slightly moist, because wet peds blur together.

soil-phys-002.title: Plates, prisms, blocks and crumbs: the shapes of structure
soil-phys-002.text: Dig a pit and the soil's architecture shows itself as plates, prisms, columns, blocks and crumbs. These are the five major soil structure types, a grouping of structure by the shape and arrangement of its peds. Platy units are flat plates, usually lying horizontally. They form mainly in subsoil packed down by trampling or machinery, and they hinder water and roots heading downward. Prismatic units stand tall, with flat to rounded vertical faces and flat tops. They typify B horizons enriched with clay washed down from above, split apart by freezing and thawing and by wetting and drying. Columnar units resemble prisms with distinct, rounded tops. Common in subsoils rich in sodium or swelling clay, they are so dense that roots struggle to enter. Blocky units are many-sided and roughly equal in every direction, common in subsoils and clay-rich topsoils. They are angular when faces meet at sharp angles and subangular when corners are mostly rounded. Granular or crumb units are nearly round, with irregular faces that do not mold to their neighbors. They dominate organic-rich grassland and garden topsoils and give good porosity. Some soils also hold wedges, interlocking elliptical lenses often bounded by slickensides, polished surfaces where soil slid past soil. Lenticular units are overlapping lenses parallel to the surface, typical of moist, silty soils prone to frost action. Size classes shift with shape. Very coarse means over 10 mm for platy and granular peds, over 50 mm for blocky ones and over 100 mm for prisms.

soil-phys-006.title: Flocculation: how clay plates cling together
soil-phys-006.text: Clay plates carry a quirk of charge, with slightly positive edges and negative faces, so edge sticks to face. That is flocculation, the drawing together of primary soil particles into microscopic clumps called floccules. Van der Waals forces, electrostatic forces and hydrogen bonds do the pulling. The opposite is dispersion, and soil pH, electrical conductivity and sodium content set the balance. Sodium that displaces polyvalent cations, positive ions with several charges, deflocculates the clay. Floccules last only once cementing agents stabilize them.

soil-phys-005.title: Soil aggregation: turning loose grains into lasting crumbs
soil-phys-005.text: Earthworms, fungi, frost and chemistry all work on the same project: turning loose grains into crumbs. Soil aggregation is the joining of primary soil particles into larger aggregates through rearrangement, flocculation and cementation. Flocculated clumps become true aggregates only once something cements them. Carbonates, gypsum, clay particles, organic matter and sesquioxides, the oxides of iron and aluminum, all serve as cement. Biofilms and fungal hyphae strengthen the bonds. So do multivalent cations bridging negatively charged particles, and hydrogen and hydrophobic bonds between organic compounds. Calcium bridges clay and organic matter. It can also replace sodium on particle surfaces, curbing the dispersion, crusting and bursting of crumbs that plague sodic soils. The best glue depends on the clay. Organic matter is the main binder with swelling 2:1 clays such as montmorillonite, met in {{ref:soil-phys-029}}. With oxides and 1:1 clays such as kaolinite, electrostatic bonds join in, and aggregation is weaker. Sesquioxides cement aggregates larger than 100 μm, especially in soils with more than 10% sesquioxides. Weather shuffles the pieces. Wetting and drying, and shrinking and swelling, rearrange particles and can either strengthen or weaken aggregates. Freezing wet soil breaks aggregates into smaller ones. Some shrink-swell soils even mulch themselves, building a granular surface through repeated shrinking and swelling. Life builds aggregates too, through earthworm casts, the fecal pellets of mites and collembola, roots and fungal hyphae. These biological agents matter most where swelling 2:1 clays are lacking.

soil-phys-007.title: Crumbs within crumbs: the aggregate hierarchy
soil-phys-007.text: A soil crumb is usually built of smaller crumbs, which are built of smaller ones still. The aggregate hierarchy is the idea that aggregates form in levels, larger and looser ones made from smaller, denser ones. Particles join into microaggregates below 250 μm, and these into macroaggregates above 250 μm. Fungal hyphae and roots, the temporary binders, hold macroaggregates together. Transient polysaccharides and persistent compounds hold microaggregates. Yet organic matter's role is hard to pin down, and in some soils it is not the main binder.

soil-phys-004.title: Aggregate stability: will the crumbs survive
soil-phys-004.text: Building crumbs is half the job, and keeping them is the other half. Soil aggregate stability measures how well aggregates resist breaking apart under erosion, shrinking and swelling, and tillage. Because it blends physical, chemical and biological properties and responds to management, it makes a useful soil-quality indicator. Stability directly controls the spread of pore sizes. In well-aggregated soil, tiny micropores store water while larger pores let water and air move in. Such soils usually take in water faster and rarely pond. In compacted soil, with few aggregates and little pore space, roots grow poorly and can be cut off from stored water. Tillage and the traffic of machines and livestock are the main disruptors, and heavy or irregular rain can also do harm. Reduced or zero tillage, cover crops, perennial crops and organic inputs have been shown to improve aggregation.

soil-phys-008.title: Sieving and soaking: testing how tough crumbs are
soil-phys-008.text: Soil crumbs are tested the way nature attacks them, with water or with wind. Aggregate stability measurement covers tests of how well aggregates survive such stresses, or those of machinery. Wet methods usually matter more, because they mimic water erosion. Wet sieving turns slowly wetted 2-4 mm aggregates in a sieve nest at 30 rotations per minute for about 10 minutes. It reports a mean weight diameter. Arid regions, where wind erosion dominates, use a dry method that sieves 0.92-1.68 mm aggregates and reports the share above 0.42 mm.

soil-phys-009.title: Slaking: when trapped air bursts soil crumbs
soil-phys-009.text: Drop a dry crumb of soil into water, and the air trapped inside can blow it apart. That is slaking, the break-up of aggregates when entering water displaces air from pores and bursts aggregates holding trapped air. It is purely mechanical, one of the direct ways water destroys soil structure. In the field, slaking follows raindrop impact, so ground cover protects against both. Stable aggregates resist it, along with crusting and erosion. In sodic soils, calcium that replaces sodium on particle surfaces eases slaking, dispersion and crusting alike.

soil-phys-033.title: Soil dispersion: how sodium makes clay wash away
soil-phys-033.text: A dispersive soil can look perfectly sound until digging lets running water reach it. Soil dispersion is the breakdown of soil, especially sodium-rich clay, into separate fine particles that water easily washes away. It is the opposite of flocculation, and soil pH, electrical conductivity and sodium content control both. Sodium drives the damage. At high levels, sodium ions break clay platelets apart, so wet particles repel one another and aggregates fall to pieces. Calcium and magnesium do the reverse, promoting flocculation. The key gauge is the exchangeable sodium percentage, sodium's share of all the cations a soil holds. Above 5%, dispersion becomes possible, and above 15% it is highly likely. Dispersive layers usually hide in the subsoil, where clay and sodium concentrate. They feel soapy and often have prismatic or columnar structure. Such soils are commoner in old landscapes, and sodium collects low in the landscape. Once exposed, dispersed soil feeds gully and tunnel erosion, degrades structure and turns water turbid. Where the particles settle, they clog and seal the surface. Irrigation can bring the same collapse, as aggregates break down and clay disperses on rapid wetting. Management is mostly restraint: avoid disturbance, keep vegetation cover and control salt. Where the soil has already been disturbed, gypsum is added.

soil-phys-011.title: Hardsetting soil: soft when wet, hard as it dries
soil-phys-011.text: Some soils go soft in the rain, then dry too hard to push a forefinger into. A hardsetting soil loses its structure when wet and sets into a hard, structureless mass as it dries. Cracks are few, usually more than 0.1 m apart. It is not permanently cemented: after flood irrigation or one intense rain, it softens and then sets hard again. Such soil can be tilled only in a narrow moisture range, and it sheds rain as runoff. It runs deeper than a crust, often as thick as the cultivated layer.

soil-phys-031.title: Soil crust: the hard surface that turns rain away
soil-phys-031.text: When rain will not soak into bare ground, the culprit is usually the surface itself. A soil crust is a surface layer, often hardened and platy, that differs from the bulk soil beneath it. Physical crusts form under the impact of raindrops or trampling. Salts and silica collect in them, so they are often harder than uncrusted soil. They cut infiltration, the soaking of water into soil, hinder plants trying to establish and erode quickly once broken. In arid and semi-arid regions, intense rain soon outpaces a sealed surface, and the excess runs off overland. Better soil structure means less crusting and better seedling emergence. Coarse organic matter left on the surface helps prevent crusts, and on sodic soils so does calcium swapped for sodium. Other crusts are alive, formed by communities of surface microorganisms, the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-032}}.

soil-phys-032.title: Biological soil crust: the living skin of deserts
soil-phys-032.text: Even in deserts, the ground can be alive at its very surface. A biological soil crust is a living community of organisms forming a crust on the soil in arid and semi-arid ecosystems. Cyanobacteria, lichens and mosses build it, capturing and storing a significant amount of carbon by photosynthesis. The crust also fixes nitrogen, stabilizes soil and changes how much sunlight the surface reflects. Fire, grazing, recreation and other disturbance damage it, and recovery can take a long time.

soil-phys-010.title: Rebuilding the crumb: how farmers repair soil structure
soil-phys-010.text: Each extra millimeter of rain that good structure lets soak in can add 10 kg/ha to a wheat yield. Improving soil structure means practices that push soil toward a granular, crumb structure. They raise porosity, organic matter and the activity of microbes and soil animals. The rewards are less erosion, more water soaking in, easier rooting and fewer crusts blocking seedlings. Mulch, manure and compost, practiced since people first settled to farm, build stable bridges between mineral particles. Where warm, moist climates break down organic matter too fast, charcoal served instead, as in pre-Columbian terra preta. Biochar is the modern version. Lime helps because divalent calcium bridges negatively charged clay and organic molecules. Advisers urge pasture phases in rotations, less tillage and ground cover against raindrops. On irrigated sodic soils, gypsum lets calcium displace sodium. Less tillage is no cure-all, though: in irrigated horticulture, no-till usually loses productivity as structure degrades.

soil-phys-039.title: Tilth: what makes soil fit for a crop
soil-phys-039.text: By one 2021 estimate, tillage turns 1840 km3 of soil a year worldwide, against 960 km3 moved by plant roots and earthworms. All that plowing chases tilth, the physical condition of a soil, especially how well it suits planting and growing a crop. Soil in good tilth is spongy, with large pores for air and water and a reasonable store of water and nutrients. Its aggregates are strong enough to hold together yet friable, crumbling readily under shallow tilling. Too much strength yields large cemented clods. Tilth depends on stable aggregates, moisture, air and soil life, and it can change quickly. Tillage improves it only briefly, and long-term plowing tends to compact the soil. The most stable tilth comes from life: substances released by roots feed bacteria that secrete polysaccharides, and fungi whose hyphae bind particles. Grass and legume sods, deep-rooted perennials such as alfalfa, and cover crops help rebuild compacted soil.

soil-phys-041.title: Soil consistency: how soil feels between the fingers
soil-phys-041.text: Squeeze a moist lump between thumb and finger, and its resistance says a good deal about the soil. Soil consistency is the ability of soil to stick to itself or to other objects and to resist deformation and rupture. It is judged air-dry, moist and wet, and in each state it depends on clay content. Dry soil is rubbed to see how it crumbles, moist soil is pressed, and wet soil is checked for stickiness and plasticity. Standard terms run from loose to extremely hard when dry, and from nonsticky to very sticky when wet. Cemented soils barely change with moisture, and the most cemented, called indurated, need hammer blows to break. Because these judgments rest on feel, they are close to subjective. Still, consistency roughly predicts trouble with cultivation and with supporting buildings and roads.

soil-phys-021.title: Atterberg limits: the water contents where soil changes state
soil-phys-021.text: Add water to a dry fine-grained soil, and it passes from solid to semi-solid to plastic to liquid. The Atterberg limits are the critical water contents that mark where it crosses from one of these states to the next. Albert Atterberg, a Swedish chemist and agronomist, devised them in 1911. He also proposed the first soil particle-size classification, described in {{ref:soil-phys-048}}. Arthur Casagrande, a pioneer of soil mechanics, later refined them. Because the changes are gradual, standard tests fix each boundary by convention. The first of those tests appears in {{ref:soil-phys-022}}. The tests suit clayey and silty soils, which shrink, swell and change strength as their moisture varies. Fine-grained soils are classified mainly by these limits rather than by grain size. The limits are simple to measure and closely tied to compressibility, permeability and strength, so they offer quick estimates of all three.

soil-phys-022.title: Liquid limit: where clay starts to flow
soil-phys-022.text: Twenty-five drops of a cup can hint at whether a clay will swell. The liquid limit is the water content at which a clayey soil stops behaving as a plastic solid and starts behaving as a liquid. In Casagrande's cup test, it is the moisture content at which 25 drops close a groove cut in the soil over 12.7 mm. Europe prefers the fall cone test, which measures how far a steel cone sinks. Values over 50 suggest significant swelling. The same value of 50 divides high- from low-plasticity fine soils in {{ref:soil-phys-036}}.

soil-phys-023.title: Plastic limit: the thread that breaks at 3.2 mm
soil-phys-023.text: A standard soil test needs little more than a rolled thread of soil. The plastic limit is the water content below which a soil turns brittle and can no longer be rolled into a thin thread. Rolled on a flat, non-porous surface, the thread breaks at larger diameters as it dries. The limit is the moisture content, by weight, at which it breaks apart at 3.2 mm, about 1/8 inch. A soil that never reaches 3.2 mm at any moisture is non-plastic. Remolded soil here is quite stiff, near 200 kPa of undrained shear strength.

soil-phys-024.title: Shrinkage limit: the point where drying clay stops shrinking
soil-phys-024.text: A drying clay shrinks, but only up to a point. The shrinkage limit is the water content below which further drying no longer makes a soil shrink. It is used much less often than the liquid and plastic limits. Its value depends on the clay mineral. Reported shrinkage limits run 8.5–15% for montmorillonite, 15–17% for illite and 25–29% for kaolinite. So kaolinite stops shrinking while it still holds far more water than montmorillonite does.

soil-phys-025.title: Plasticity index: the span where soil stays moldable
soil-phys-025.text: One subtraction turns two lab tests into a telling measure of a clay. The plasticity index is the span of water contents over which a soil behaves plastically: the liquid limit minus the plastic limit. A score of 0 means non-plastic, below 7 slightly plastic, 7–17 medium plastic, and above 17 highly plastic. The index tracks permeability, compressibility and shear strength. Above 35, it signals high expansion potential. Silts and clays are sorted by plotting this index against the liquid limit, the method of {{ref:soil-phys-036}}.

soil-phys-026.title: Liquidity index: where a soil's water sits between limits
soil-phys-026.text: Where a soil's natural water content, W, falls between its limits says much about how strong it is once remolded. The liquidity index places W on the scale from plastic to liquid limit: LI = (W − PL)/(LL − PL). At 0 the soil sits at its plastic limit, near 200 kPa of undrained shear strength. At 1 it sits at its liquid limit, with only about 2 kPa. A companion consistency index, (LL − W)/(LL − PL), runs the other way, and the two always add up to 1.

soil-phys-027.title: Clay activity: same clay content, different behavior
soil-phys-027.text: Two soils with the same amount of clay can behave very differently, because clay minerals differ. Clay activity is the ratio of a soil's plasticity index to its clay-size fraction, used to judge how active its clay is. Below 0.75 the clay is inactive, above 1.25 active, and in between normal. Montmorillonite has liquid limits of 100–900%, against 60–120% for illite and 30–110% for kaolinite. The ratio links clay as a size to clay as a mineral, the split explained in {{ref:soil-phys-054}}.

soil-phys-036.title: The Unified Soil Classification System: soil in two letters
soil-phys-036.text: Engineers across North America describe a soil with just two letters. Those letters come from the Unified Soil Classification System, or USCS, which classes soils by texture and grain size. It is the most common engineering classification in North America and works for most unconsolidated materials. The first letter names the main material: G for gravel, S for sand, M for silt, C for clay and O for organic soil. Peat gets PT. The second letter gives grading, W for well graded or P for poorly graded, or liquid limit, H for high and L for low. Soils fall into three major groups: coarse-grained sands and gravels, fine-grained silts and clays, and highly organic soils, or peat. Sieves draw the first line. A soil is coarse-grained if more than 50% stays on the No. 200 sieve, whose openings are 0.075 mm. The No. 4 sieve, with 4.75 mm openings, separates sand from gravel. Under the USCS, silt particles measure 0.002–0.075 mm and sand particles 0.075–4.75 mm. Sands and gravels are then divided by grain size and grading. Silts and clays are divided by their Atterberg limits into high- and low-plasticity soils. With 5–12% fines, the silt and clay particles, both grading and plasticity count. A dual symbol may then appear, such as GW-GM for well-graded gravel with silt. Europe's ISO 14688 is very similar but adds an intermediate-plasticity class for silts and clays.

soil-phys-037.title: Gravels and sands: the USCS coarse-grained groups
soil-phys-037.text: In the USCS, a soil is coarse when more than half its weight stays on the No. 200 sieve. It is gravel (G) if more than 50% of its coarse fraction stays on the No. 4 sieve, and sand (S) otherwise. Clean gravels and sands, under 5% fines, are well graded (GW, SW) or poorly graded (GP, SP). GW needs Cu ≥ 4 and SW Cu ≥ 6, both with 1 ≤ Cc ≤ 3. Above 12% fines they become silty (GM, SM) or clayey (GC, SC), and in between they take dual symbols such as SW-SC.

soil-phys-038.title: Silts and clays: the USCS fine-grained groups
soil-phys-038.text: Once at least half a soil passes the No. 200 sieve, grain size stops deciding its name. Such soils are classed as silts (M) or clays (C) by plotting plasticity index against liquid limit. The A-line splits clays from silts, and a liquid limit of 50% splits high (H) from low (L) plasticity. The inorganic groups are lean clay (CL), silt (ML), fat clay (CH) and elastic silt (MH). CL needs a plasticity index above 7, and ML one below 4. Organic silts and clays (OL, OH) are told apart by changes on oven drying.

soil-phys-034.title: Hydrophobic soil: ground that sheds water
soil-phys-034.text: Fire can leave behind soil that sheds water instead of soaking it up. A hydrophobic soil is one whose particles repel water. It most often forms when fire or hot air drives waxy compounds out of surface litter to coat sandy particles below. Sand is most prone because its large grains have little surface area and are easily coated. Repellency slows infiltration, so runoff and erosion rise, and Australia has seen production losses of up to 80%. Adding clay helps: calcium-bentonite raised one barley yield from 1.7 to 3.4 t/ha.

soil-phys-035.title: Timing a water drop: measuring how much soil repels water
soil-phys-035.text: The simplest measure of a stubborn soil is how long one drop of water takes to soak in. Soil water repellency tests rate how strongly a soil repels water, usually starting with that drop. Under 5 seconds means not repellent, up to 1 minute slightly repellent, 1–10 minutes repellent, and longer severely repellent. The molarity of ethanol droplet test tries ethanol solutions of falling surface tension until one soaks in within 10 seconds. An index of 1 or less means non-repellent, and 2.2 or more severely repellent.

soil-phys-042.title: Soil resistivity: how soil resists electric current
soil-phys-042.text: Soil carries electric current, and how easily it does so affects how fast buried metal and concrete corrode. Soil resistivity is a measure of how strongly a soil resists the flow of that current. Wetter soil, or soil with a higher electrolyte concentration, has lower resistivity. Current then flows more easily, and corrosion speeds up. Values typically range from about 1 to 100,000 Ω·m. Saline soils sit at the low end, and dry soils over crystalline rocks at the high end.

reviews.soil-texture-and-structure: Texture, the mix of sand, silt and clay, is fixed by the mineral particles, but structure is how those particles clump into peds and aggregates. Coatings of iron oxides, carbonates, clay, silica and humus bind the crumbs, and their pattern of pores steers water, air and roots. Unlike texture, structure is dynamic: tillage, traffic, sodium and rapid wetting tear it down, while roots, fungi, earthworms, lime and gypsum rebuild it. Water also sets a fine-grained soil's behavior, and the Atterberg limits mark where it shifts from solid to plastic to liquid. The USDA groups textures into twelve classes, farmers judge tilth, and engineers reach for sieves, those limits and two-letter USCS symbols.
